source_refs.note: 1. Monocytes: a main subheading of 21.3.1 Components of the Immune System, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 176-176.

blocks.text: They are a type of WBCs and are produced in lymphoid tissues. They circulate in blood and also enter the interstitial fluid. Here, they mature into macrophages. The macrophages phagocytose and destroy the microbes. They also produce proteins that activate the helper T cells. Monocytes also mature into other kinds of phagocytes, which remain in liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and other tissues. They also help to clear cellular debris and assist in repairing tissue damage.

blocks.alt: A human body outline with the organs of the immune system: tonsils and adenoids in the throat, lymph nodes in the neck, armpits and groin, lymphatic vessels joining them, the thymus in the chest, the spleen on the left side of the abdomen, the appendix, and bone marrow in the thigh bones.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says monocytes are produced in lymphoid tissues. In fact monocytes, like the other white blood cells (as the book says at the start of this topic), are produced in the bone marrow, from myeloid stem cells.
